value.claim_en: Russians have not admitted that the Shelling of Mainila was staged by the Soviet Union, and Soviet responsibility for the incident remains historically disputed.
value.claim_fi: Venäläiset eivät ole myöntäneet Mainilan laukausten olleen Neuvostoliiton lavastama hyökkäys, ja tapahtuman luonne on edelleen historiallisesti kiistanalainen.
value.narrative_en: Soviet/Russian denial of staging the Shelling of Mainila
value.historical_note_en: Mainstream historical consensus, supported by later admissions from Soviet and Russian leaders including Nikita Khrushchev and Boris Yeltsin as well as Russian historians in the 1990s, is that the Red Army staged the Shelling of Mainila as a pretext for the Winter War.
value.uncertainty_note: The diff appears to aggregate multiple back-and-forth edits in an edit war, and the edit also involves source manipulation (keeping the Yle source attached to the opposite claim while adding an unreliable Russian web source) and a false factual claim regarding Russian admissions.

value.what_changed_en: Inserted an unsourced assertion stating "However, this does not hold true" regarding a sourced estimate of Simo Häyhä's sniper kills, and added a rifle serial number ("serial number 35281") elsewhere in the article without citations.
evidence: paras kun ei julista ettei pidä paikkaansa, sillä uhriluvut vaikea todistaa
value.claim_en: A cited estimate of Simo Häyhä's kill count is untrue, and one of his weapons had the serial number 35281.
value.claim_fi: Eräs lähteistetty arvio Simo Häyhän uhriluvusta ei pidä paikkaansa, ja hänen aseensa sarjanumero oli 35281.
value.narrative_en: Debating Simo Häyhä's exact sniper kill count
value.uncertainty_note: The context window cuts off where the serial number was inserted and does not show the exact placement of 'Tämä ei kuitenkaan pidä paikkaansa' (whether it dismissed the ~542 figure or the ~200 figure); depending on which estimate was flatly rejected, this also borders on pov_push or content_dispute.

value.what_changed_en: Reverted an anonymous user's angry commentary embedded in the article text (complaining about a 'leftist researcher' claiming 200 kills instead of over 500) and restored the statement that a more accurate estimate of Simo Häyhä's kills is likely around 200 soldiers. The edit appears to be part of an ongoing edit war, and the inserted text seems to contain a partial duplication ('joskin oikeampi arvio lienee noin').
evidence: , joskin oikeampi arvio lienee noin 200 sotilasta
value.claim_en: A more accurate estimate of the number of soldiers shot by Simo Häyhä is around 200 rather than 542.
value.claim_fi: Oikeampi arvio Simo Häyhän ampumien sotilaiden määrästä on noin 200 eikä 542.
value.narrative_en: Debate over Simo Häyhä's actual sniper kill count
value.uncertainty_note: The edit summary combines multiple automated revert summaries, suggesting the dataset merged consecutive edits/reverts in an ongoing edit war; the edit itself restored sourced content over disruptive commentary, and its subsequent reversion 11 days later may have been by another edit warrior or to fix the duplicated fragment.

value.what_changed_en: Changed the demolition year of Vehmainen railway station from 1998 to 2000, added that bullet marks are also visible in window frames ('sekä ikkunanpielissä'), capitalised 'ortodoksikirkon' ('Orthodox church'), and removed a 'citation needed' tag ('{{lähde}}') without providing a source.
value.claim_en: Vehmainen railway station was demolished in 2000, and bullet impacts from the 1918 Battle of Tampere are visible in the window frames as well as the walls of several local buildings.
value.claim_fi: Vehmaisten asema purettiin vuonna 2000, ja Tampereen taistelun luotien iskeymiä on nähtävissä rakennusten seinien lisäksi myös ikkunanpielissä.
value.uncertainty_note: It is unclear whether the editor sincerely believed the station was demolished in 2000 (making it an unsourced good-faith edit that improperly removed a citation-needed tag and introduced capitalisation/punctuation errors) or deliberately altered the date as subtle vandalism.

value.what_changed_en: An anonymous editor reverted a previous cleanup edit in the article's infobox, restoring a list of specific Finnish regions (South Karelia, Ladoga Karelia, North Karelia, Kainuu, Lapland) under battle locations, altering C. G. E. Mannerheim's display name to Gustaf Mannerheim, and changing link formatting and line breaks.
evidence: Carl Gustaf Emil Mannerheim|C. G. E.
value.uncertainty_note: Because only the diff tokens are visible and the edit is a revert of a previous revision, it is unclear whether the anonymous editor was defending their own good-faith infobox formatting/detail preferences or restoring broken wikitext markup.

value.what_changed_en: Changed the battle's outcome from one destroyed Soviet division to plural "divisions", increased Soviet casualties from 17,500 to 20,000, and attempted to add an improperly formatted citation citing "Markus Juutila: Winter War book, documentaries, my grandfather's stories" alongside a {{Lähde}} ('citation needed') template.
evidence: Markus Juutila: talvisota kirja, dokumentit, isoisäni kertomukset.
value.claim_en: Multiple Soviet divisions were destroyed in the Battle of Raate Road, and Soviet casualties numbered 20,000.
value.claim_fi: Raatteen tien taistelussa tuhottiin useita Neuvostoliiton divisioonia ja neuvostotappiot olivat 20 000 miestä.
value.historical_note_en: Only one Soviet division (the 44th Rifle Division) was destroyed on the Raate Road itself; the 163rd Rifle Division was defeated earlier in the broader Battle of Suomussalmi, and wartime estimates of over 20,000 dead on Raate Road have been revised sharply downward by modern historians (who also note the author's name is Antti Juutilainen, not Markus Juutila).
value.uncertainty_note: Could also be classified as false_factual_claim, as it alters specific casualty and unit numbers based on misremembered sources and family lore, though the naive attempt to cite sources using the {{Lähde}} button strongly indicates an inexperienced good-faith editor.

value.what_changed_en: Added a new subsection titled "Linija Mannergeima" containing a list of unformatted YouTube links (Parts I–VIII, with Part I duplicated) to the 1940 Soviet documentary film already mentioned in the preceding paragraph.
value.uncertainty_note: Could also be classified under 'other' as external link spam, though it appears to be a sincere attempt to provide video links for the historical Soviet documentary discussed right above it, violating Wikipedia style and external link/copyright guidelines.

value.what_changed_en: Reworded Simo Häyhä's sniper kill count from 'up to 542 men, though a more accurate estimate is likely around 200 soldiers' to 'from about 200 men up to 542 fallen enemy soldiers', removing the preference for the lower figure, and added a sentence citing The Telegraph that other sources report 505 kills.
evidence: jopa 542 miestä, joskin oikeampi arvio lienee noin 200 sotilasta.
noin 200 miehestä jopa 542 kaadettuun vihollisen sotilaaseen asti.
Toisto pois + ks. keskustelu uhriluvusta. | palautus, Ks.lähdekritiikki keskustelusivulta
value.claim_en: Estimates of the number of soldiers killed by Simo Häyhä range equally from 200 to 542, with other sources reporting 505.
value.claim_fi: Arviot Simo Häyhän kaatamien sotilaiden määrästä vaihtelevat noin 200 miehestä 542 sotilaaseen, ja toiset lähteet ilmoittavat luvuksi 505.
value.narrative_en: Emphasising higher sniper kill counts for Simo Häyhä
value.uncertainty_note: The edit shifts emphasis toward the higher, popularised kill counts (505/542) over critical academic estimates (~200) and uses the term 'vihollisen' (enemy), bordering on mild pov_push or good_faith_error regarding source criticism, though the revert summary treats it as a talk-page sourcing and repetition dispute.

value.what_changed_en: Inserted a conversational, joking comment with a winking emoticon into the article text, noting that cans of herring and blankets sent by the Portuguese had clearly been forgotten.
evidence: *Täällähän on selkeästi unohdettu Portugalilaisten lähettämät sillipurkit ja huovat... ;)*
value.claim_en: Portugal sent cans of herring and blankets to Finland during the Winter War.
value.claim_fi: Portugali lähetti Suomeen sillipurkkeja ja huopia talvisodan aikana.
value.uncertainty_note: It is ambiguous whether this should be classified as a good_faith_error (an inexperienced user treating the article like a talk page to point out missing historical aid—Portugal did send humanitarian aid including canned sardines/fish and clothing) or light vandalism/joke graffiti due to the informal tone and winking emoticon.

value.what_changed_en: Added detailed Soviet casualty figures for the Battle of Raate Road (6,450 total excluding frostbite and illness, including 1,150 from the 3rd NKVD Regiment and 5,305 from the 44th Division), attributing them parenthetically to 'newer Russian research (K. Usva)' without providing a verifiable citation and leaving a stray word break ('miestä'). The edit was reverted for being unsourced ('Lähteetöntä').
evidence: 3.NKVD-rykmentin tappiot jotka on arvioitu uudemmassa venäläistutkimuksissa (К. Усва) olleen 1 150 miestä
Kaikkiaan tutkimus arvioi Raatteentien taisteluissa neuvostotappioiksi n. 6 450 ilman paleltuneita ja sairaita.
Heistä 5 305 oli 44.Divisioonan sotilasta (1 144 kaatunutta, 1 807 haavoittunutta ja  2 354 kadonnutta
value.claim_en: Recent Russian research by K. Usva estimates Soviet casualties in the Battle of Raate Road at approximately 6,450 (excluding frostbite and illness), comprising 1,150 from the 3rd NKVD Regiment and 5,305 from the 44th Division.
value.claim_fi: Uudempi venäläistutkimus (K. Usva) arvioi neuvostotappioiksi Raatteen tien taistelussa noin 6 450 miestä ilman paleltuneita ja sairaita, joista 1 150 kuului 3. NKVD-rykmenttiin ja 5 305 44. divisioonaan.
value.uncertainty_note: 'К. Усва' (K. Usva, a Finnish-sounding name in Cyrillic) is likely an amateur internet blogger or forum researcher rather than a published historian, making this an addition of unreliable/unsourced material rather than deliberate fabrication, though verifying whether K. Usva exists at all is ambiguous.

value.what_changed_en: Added a summary to the infobox's 'result' field stating 'Soviet victory (military), Finnish defensive victory (political)', before the existing link to the Moscow Peace Treaty. The editor argued in the summary for explicitly naming winners, while the reverter cited vague concepts, lack of sources, and established editorial consensus.
evidence: Suomihan ei voinut voittaa sotilaallisesti, koska joutui vetäytymään Rajajoelta Viipurin itäreunalle, toki poliittisesti Suomi saavutti torjuntavoiton.
rv, epämääräisiä käsitteitä | lähteet ensin | Palautus - ilmeinen konsensus versiohistoriasta päätellen
value.claim_en: The Winter War resulted in a Soviet military victory and a Finnish political defensive victory.
value.claim_fi: Talvisota päättyi Neuvostoliiton sotilaalliseen voittoon ja Suomen poliittiseen torjuntavoittoon.
value.uncertainty_note: Could also be viewed as good_faith_error (unsourced synthesis violating infobox consensus) or mild pov_push regarding the 'torjuntavoitto' framing, though the editor explicitly includes both Soviet military victory and Finnish defensive victory in an attempt at balance.

value.what_changed_en: Removed the sourced statement that the Shelling of Mainila was a Soviet false-flag attack later admitted by Russians, replacing it with conditional wording ('might have been') and unsourced speculation that Finland could theoretically have fired the shots with light mortars. It also framed the alleged casualties as giving grounds for ending the non-aggression pact.
evidence: Todellisuudessa kyseessä oli, kuten venäläisetkin ovat myöhemmin myöntäneet,
teoriassa on mahdollista, että myös Suomi saattoi olla todellisuudessa laukausten takana.
vetosi nootissaan kaatuneisiin sotilaihin, mikä antoi perusteet
value.claim_en: Soviet responsibility for the Shelling of Mainila is uncertain and not admitted by Russia, and Finland could theoretically have carried out the shelling using light mortars.
value.claim_fi: Neuvostoliiton syyllisyys Mainilan laukauksiin on epävarmaa eikä Venäjä ole myöntänyt osallisuuttaan, ja teoriassa myös Suomi saattoi ampua laukaukset kevyillä kranaatinheittimillä.
value.narrative_en: Soviet/Russian revisionist framing of the Shelling of Mainila and Winter War outbreak
value.historical_note_en: Historians have established that the Shelling of Mainila on 26 November 1939 was a false-flag provocation staged by the Soviet Union as a pretext to invade Finland, a conclusion supported by Finnish border observations, Soviet archival evidence, and acknowledgements by Soviet and Russian leaders including Boris Yeltsin.
value.uncertainty_note: The edit also removes a Yle citation while claiming in the edit summary that the source did not support Russian admission, so source_manipulation is a strong secondary aspect alongside pov_push and false_factual_claim.

value.what_changed_en: Made stylistic, formatting, and citation template cleanups across the article, while also filling in the unknown Soviet commander in the infobox as 'Major General Maxim Romanov' (Kenraalimajuri Maxim Romanov) and accidentally duplicating a raw book reference line in the body text.
evidence: Onni Kajaste Talvisodan Ääniä kustantaja Karisto [[ISBN 951-23-1697-8]]
value.claim_en: Major General Maxim Romanov was the Soviet commander in the Battle of Kollaa.
value.claim_fi: Kenraalimajuri Maxim Romanov oli neuvostoliittolainen komentaja Kollaan taistelussa.
value.uncertainty_note: Without a revert summary or full context around the inserted text, it is unclear whether the edit was reverted because 'Maxim Romanov' was considered inaccurate/imprecise (Mikhail Romanov commanded the 56th Rifle Division early on, while Grigory Shtern and Vladimir Kurdyumov commanded the 8th Army), or because the editor accidentally pasted a raw citation string into the body text and broke date links like '[[9' / 'maaliskuuta]].'.

value.what_changed_en: Added unsourced details to a previously cited section about Simo Häyhä's rifle serial number (35281) and his lack of experience with scoped rifles, including a claim that he refused a captured Soviet m/91-30 PE sniper rifle during the Battle of Kollaa. The edit was reverted because it inserted unverified claims into a sourced passage where the cited reference did not support the new text.
evidence: Kollaan taisteluiden aikana hänelle tarjottiin sotasaaliiksi saatua neuvostoliittolaista m/91-30 PE-kiikarikivääriä, mutta Häyhä ei halunnut ottaa kiikarikivääriä käyttöön.
lähteistetty tekstiosuus jonka lähteessä tätä ei ole
value.claim_en: Simo Häyhä's rifle had serial number 35281, he had no prior experience with scoped rifles, and he declined an offer to use a captured Soviet m/91-30 PE sniper rifle at Kollaa to avoid learning a new weapon system under fire.
value.claim_fi: Simo Häyhän kiväärin sarjanumero oli 35281, hänellä ei ollut aiempaa kokemusta kiikarikivääreistä ja hän kieltäytyi Kollaalla sotasaaliiksi saadusta neuvostoliittolaisesta m/91-30 PE -kiikarikivääristä välttääkseen uuden asejärjestelmän opettelun tulen alla.
value.uncertainty_note: Adding unsourced text inside a cited paragraph also causes text-source integrity issues (overlapping with source_manipulation), though the neutral tone and edit summary ('Added information') strongly indicate a sincere good-faith contribution rather than deliberate misrepresentation.

value.what_changed_en: Inserted unsourced text into the lead paragraph (with typos and broken sentence structure) stating that the name 'Mannerheim Line' was coined by foreign journalists covering the Winter War and was not used in official Finnish terminology; the reverter removed it as unsourced.
evidence: talvisodasta kertovat ulkomaalaiset sanomalehtimiehet antoivat nimityksen ''Mannerheim-linja''
Suomen virallisessa kielenkäytössä ei linjaa kutsuttu Mannerheim-linajaksi.
value.claim_en: The name 'Mannerheim Line' was coined by foreign journalists covering the Winter War and was not used in official Finnish terminology.
value.claim_fi: Nimen Mannerheim-linja antoivat talvisodasta kertoneet ulkomaalaiset toimittajat, eikä nimitystä käytetty Suomen virallisessa kielenkäytössä.
value.historical_note_en: While the official Finnish military term was 'pääasema' (main position) and the international press popularised 'Mannerheim Line' during the Winter War, the name is generally attributed to the Finnish artist Jorma Gallen-Kallela in autumn 1939 before the war broke out.
value.uncertainty_note: Could also be classified as false_factual_claim regarding who coined the name, as it directly contradicted the second paragraph attributing the name to Jorma Gallen-Kallela, though the editor's main intent seems to be a sincere but unsourced and poorly formatted clarification that the term was journalistic rather than official.

value.what_changed_en: Replaced the infobox details of the Battle of Raate Road with a fictional Joke battle ('Mannestan's last battle' / 'The Lempäälä rebellion'), incorporating ethnic slurs ('Manne' for Romani people, 'Nekke' as a racial slur) and vulgarities ('Kyrvätaistelu' meaning 'Cock battle'), while deleting citations.
value.uncertainty_note: The removed text contains fragments ('The Lempäälä rebellion', '518') from an immediately preceding vandalistic edit by the same user, as indicated by the revert summary reverting the last two edits.

value.what_changed_en: Added a claim disputing that the Red Army gave Simo Häyhä the nickname 'White Death', stating instead that many claim it originated on the Finnish side and became popular at the earliest on December 21, 1939 when he got 25 kills in one day. The edit cited an incomplete English-language video or episode title, admitted in the edit summary that not everything written may be 100% true, and also reverted an intermediate vandal edit ('ban xrocker', 'simo häyhä oli myös mailman sota 1').
evidence: Tästä ei kuitenkaan olla varmoja ja moni jopa väittää lempinimen tulleen Suomen puolelta, ja tulleen suosituksi aikaisintaan 21.12.1939 sinä päivänä jona Häyhä sai 25 tappoa yhdessä päivässä.
<ref>{{Jaksoviite|Nimi=What Really Happened When Soviets Invaded Finland (The Winter War)|Kieli=fi-FI}}</ref>
Voi olla että kaikki mitä kirjoitin ei ole 100% totta mutta suurin osa siitä pitäisi olla
value.claim_en: It is uncertain whether the Red Army named Simo Häyhä 'White Death', and many claim the nickname came wholly from the Finnish side, becoming popular at the earliest on December 21, 1939, when he achieved 25 kills in a single day.
value.claim_fi: Ei ole varmaa, antoiko puna-armeija Simo Häyhälle lempinimen ”Valkoinen kuolema”, ja moni väittää nimen tulleen kokonaan Suomen puolelta ja nousseen suosioon aikaisintaan 21.12.1939, jolloin hän sai 25 tappoa yhdessä päivässä.
value.narrative_en: Debunking Winter War folklore surrounding Simo Häyhä
value.uncertainty_note: The diff appears to bundle six consecutive edits (including intermediate IP vandalism and its revert). While the historical claim that 'White Death' originated in Finnish wartime press rather than among Soviet soldiers is supported by recent Finnish historians (such as Tapio Saarelainen), the editor cited a poorly formatted, likely YouTube video source, used weasel words ('moni jopa väittää'), and openly admitted uncertainty about accuracy in the summary, making 'good_faith_error' the best fit over 'content_dispute'.

value.what_changed_en: Using a revert tool, this edit replaced an ungrammatical sentence about the film The Winter War with an older vandalised version listing absurdly fabricated casualty numbers ('LOSSES finland 12 sovet union 992129').
value.claim_en: In the Battle of Taipale, Finland suffered 12 casualties and the Soviet Union suffered 992,129 casualties.
value.claim_fi: Taipaleen taistelussa Suomen tappiot olivat 12 ja Neuvostoliiton tappiot 992 129.
value.narrative_en: Exaggerating Finnish military prowess in the Winter War
value.historical_note_en: In the Battle of Taipale, Finnish casualties were over two thousand dead and several thousand wounded, while Soviet casualties were in the tens of thousands, nowhere near a million.
value.uncertainty_note: The edit summary indicates an automated undo of an IP edit ('Kumottu muokkaus...'), meaning this editor likely accidentally restored prior joke/vandalism text while reverting another problematic edit, rather than authoring the vandalism directly.

value.what_changed_en: Changed the spelling of "Raatteen tie" (Raate Road) from two words to a compound word ("Raatteentie") in several inflected forms, claiming to fix typos. The reverter undid this and instructed the editor to justify any name change on the talk page.
evidence: Perustele keskustelu-sivulla jos haluat muuttaa artikkelin nimeä
value.claim_en: Raate Road is spelled as a single compound word (Raatteentie) rather than two separate words (Raatteen tie).
value.claim_fi: Raatteen tie kirjoitetaan yhteen muodossa Raatteentie eikä erikseen.
value.uncertainty_note: Both 'Raatteen tie' (historically descriptive 'road of Raate') and 'Raatteentie' (modern official road name) exist in Finnish usage; this could also be seen as a minor stylistic content_dispute, though changing the text to contradict the article title without discussion fits good_faith_error best.

value.what_changed_en: Added an external link in the 'See also / External links' ('Aiheesta muualla') section to a user-editable wiki (maailmapalaa.net) hosting text from 'Kansan valta', the newspaper published by the Terijoki Government. It was reverted for linking to a non-authoritative website.
evidence: * [http://www.maailmapalaa.net/index.php/Kansanvalta_lehti Terijoen hallituksen julkaiseman Kansan valta lehti]
value.claim_en: The Terijoki Government published a newspaper called Kansan valta.
value.claim_fi: Terijoen hallitus julkaisi Kansan valta -nimistä lehteä.
value.uncertainty_note: If the anonymous editor was affiliated with maailmapalaa.net and adding links across multiple articles to drive traffic, 'other' (link spam) would be a closer fit.

value.what_changed_en: Replaced "Terijoen" in the name of the Terijoki Government with "Apinoiden" ("of Monkeys") and inserted repeated Wikipedia editor toolbar placeholder tags (headings, links, bold/italic text, and nowiki tags).
value.uncertainty_note: Combines juvenile mockery ('Apinoiden' / 'Monkeys') with spamming the Wikipedia editing toolbar buttons, straddling 'vandalism' and 'test_or_nonsense'.

value.what_changed_en: Rewrote the lists of ceded territories and peace terms, updated citations (e.g., replacing amateur links with official Finlex links) and map images, changed 'non-alliance against the Soviet Union' to 'mutual non-alliance', and removed a sentence stating that Finnish troops were about to break and that Franco-British promises of aid made the USSR more willing to make peace. The edit was made by an editor using the summary 'runnygnome' and was reverted two months later solely for block evasion ('eston kiertoa').
evidence: , kun Suomen joukot olivat murtumassa ja Neuvostoliiton joukot jo lähentelivät [[Viipuri
value.claim_en: The Moscow Peace Treaty established mutual non-alliance between Finland and the Soviet Union and included specific ceded territories such as the Finnish parts of both the Sredny and Rybachy peninsulas.
value.claim_fi: Moskovan rauhansopimus sisälsi molemminpuolisen liittoutumattomuuden Suomen ja Neuvostoliiton välillä sekä tarkemmin määritellyt alueluovutukset, kuten Keski- ja Kalastajasaarennon Suomen puoleiset osat.
value.uncertainty_note: The edit itself appears to be a substantive, mostly accurate cleanup of geography, terminology (Article 3 of the treaty is indeed mutual non-aggression/non-alliance), and citations by a known banned sockpuppet ('runnygnome'), reverted strictly due to block evasion rather than content.

value.what_changed_en: Inserted a fabricated, satirical paragraph claiming that newer research shows Finns fired the Shelling of Mainila themselves as part of a 'Hitlerist conspiracy' and subsequently invaded the Soviet Union in 1939 alongside German, Namibian, and American troops.
evidence: Uudempi tutkimus on kuitenkin osoittanut, että suomalaiset itse ampuivat laukaukset osana hitlerististä salaliittoa hyökätä Neuvostoliittoon.
suomalaiset hyökkäsivät Neuvostoliitton vuonna 1939 yhdessä saksalaisten, namibialaisten ja amerikkalaisten joukkojen kanssa.
value.claim_en: Finland fired the Shelling of Mainila as part of a Hitlerist conspiracy and invaded the Soviet Union in 1939 together with German, Namibian, and American forces.
value.claim_fi: Suomalaiset ampuivat Mainilan laukaukset osana hitlerististä salaliittoa ja hyökkäsivät Neuvostoliittoon vuonna 1939 yhdessä saksalaisten, namibialaisten ja amerikkalaisten joukkojen kanssa.
value.narrative_en: Parody of Soviet/Russian propaganda regarding the Winter War
value.historical_note_en: It is well established that the Soviet Union staged the Shelling of Mainila on 26 November 1939 as a false-flag pretext to invade Finland and start the Winter War.

value.what_changed_en: Added an external link to a Blogspot blog post titled 'Ukrainians in the Winter War: unknown history 77 years ago' (with a grammatical error in Finnish) under the 'External links' section. It was reverted as a link to an unvetted blog.
evidence: Ukrainalaiset Talvisodassa: tuntematon historia 77 vuoden sitten
value.uncertainty_note: Could also be classified as 'good_faith_error' (adding a blog link against Wikipedia's external links guidelines) or 'pov_push' depending on the content of the linked blog ('ukrainiancrusade'), though 'other' explicitly covers link spam and self-promotion.

value.what_changed_en: Inserted an obscene personal graffiti sentence translating to 'This is fucking shit and I love my big brother!!!!!!' along with stray heading markup.
evidence: Tämä on yhtä vitun paskaa ja minä rakastan mun isoveljeä!!!!!!

value.what_changed_en: Replaced the question mark for the Soviet commander in the battle infobox with 'Major General maxim Romanov', added a poorly formatted bibliography section citing Onni Palaste's 1980 war novel/documentary book 'Talvisodan ääniä' ('Voices of the Winter War'), and capitalised 'maxim' to 'Maxim' elsewhere in the text.
evidence: Onni Palaste Talvisodan Ääniä kustantaja Karisto vuosi  Arvi.A Karisto OY kirjapaino hämeenlinna 1980
value.claim_en: The Soviet commander at the Battle of Kollaa was Major General Maxim Romanov.
value.claim_fi: Neuvostoliiton komentaja Kollaan taistelussa oli kenraalimajuri Maxim Romanov.
value.historical_note_en: The Soviet forces at Kollaa (part of the 8th Army, including the 56th Rifle Corps and 56th Rifle Division) were commanded by officers such as Ivan Habarov, Grigori Shtern, Ivan Cherepanov, and Maksim Yevstigneyev, whereas Onni Palaste's 'Talvisodan ääniä' is a fictionalised war novel rather than a reliable historical source for Soviet command.
value.uncertainty_note: It is clear this was a sincere but poorly formatted attempt by an inexperienced editor using a war novel as a source, though it also introduces an inaccurate/imprecise factual claim about the overall Soviet commander.

value.what_changed_en: Inserted the lowercase, informal joke phrase "ja muutama muu neuvostoliiton kaveri kuten venäjä" ("and a few other friends of the Soviet Union like Russia") into the section listing the peace treaty terms.
evidence: ja muutama muu neuvostoliiton kaveri kuten venäjä

value.what_changed_en: Made several unsourced wording and factual adjustments to the section on Nordic aid during the Winter War, including changing 'civilian flight training for Finns' in Norway to 'basic flight training for students sent from Finland', asserting that several Danish military pilots came to Finland 'without permission from their own units', and introducing a typo ('läheteyille') and broken syntax (replacing 'technical stopover' with 'Finland's').
evidence: Useat sotilaslentäjät tulivat Suomeen ilman omien yksiköidensä lupaa
value.claim_en: Students sent from Finland received basic flight training near Oslo, and several Danish military pilots came to Finland during the Winter War without permission from their own units.
value.claim_fi: Suomesta lähetetyt oppilaat saivat Oslon lähellä peruslentokoulutusta, ja useat tanskalaiset sotilaslentäjät tulivat talvisotaan ilman omien yksiköidensä lupaa.
value.historical_note_en: Danish volunteer pilots in the Winter War generally travelled to Finland with official leave from the Danish military rather than deserting without permission, and the Norwegian camp at Steinsfjorden was formally organised as civilian flight training to preserve Norway's neutrality.
value.uncertainty_note: Could also be classified as false_factual_claim due to the inaccurate claim about Danish pilots lacking permission, or content_dispute, as the revert summary gives no reason, though unsourced edits with typos and broken grammar ('Stavangerin Suomen kautta') strongly suggest a reverted good-faith attempt.

value.what_changed_en: Replaced the battle name 'Kollaan taistelu' with 'kollaasin kukka hyppelyt' ('collage's flower hoppings'), replaced sniper Simo Häyhä's name with 'äitis' ('your mom'), changed the year 1939 to 2031, and removed a link to the Red Army's 56th Division.
Added an unsourced, poorly spelled sentence claiming that a large part of the film 'The Winter War' (Talvisota) is set at the Taipaleenjoki river.
evidence: Myös suuri-osa Talvi-sota elokuvasta sijoittuu taipaleen-joelle
value.claim_en: A large part of the film The Winter War is set at the Taipaleenjoki river.
value.claim_fi: Suuri osa Talvisota-elokuvasta sijoittuu Taipaleenjoelle.
value.historical_note_en: Pekka Parikka's 1989 film Talvisota depicts Infantry Regiment 23 from Southern Ostrobothnia, which actually fought in the Battle of Taipale, though the added sentence was unencyclopedic, unsourced, and full of spelling errors.
value.uncertainty_note: The claim is actually factually true regarding the 1989 film, so this is clearly a sincere, albeit poorly formatted and misspelled, attempt to add pop-culture trivia (note also the prior un-reverted vandalism at the bottom of the context).

value.what_changed_en: Removed the mention that the Winter War was fought against the Soviet Union from the lead paragraph, and added a poorly placed note about a Japanese manga (Shiroi Majo by Naruki Nagakawa, cited via an unofficial manga aggregator site) featuring a female sniper named Häyhä. Reverted with the summary 'merkittävyys epäselvä' ('notability unclear').
evidence: Japanissa on julkaistu N<small>AGAKAWA</small> Narukin piirtämä Manga
value.claim_en: A Japanese manga drawn by Naruki Nagakawa features a female sniper named Häyhä during the Winter and Continuation Wars.
value.claim_fi: Japanissa on julkaistu Naruki Nagakawan piirtämä manga, jonka päähenkilönä on talvi- ja jatkosodassa taisteleva Häyhä-niminen naispuolinen tarkka-ampuja.
value.uncertainty_note: The removal of 'against the Soviet Union' ('[[Neuvostoliitto]]a vastaan käydyssä') is unexplained in the edit summary and could have been either an accidental editing slip or a minor intentional deletion alongside the pop-culture trivia addition.

value.what_changed_en: Inserted an uncapitalised, misspelled sentence about the notorious Finnish child murderer Jammu Siltavuori ('Uncle Jammu attacked little children and forced them into his car'), completely unrelated to the Shelling of Mainila.
evidence: jammu setä hyökkäsi pikku lapsien kimppuun ja pakotti hiedät autoonsa

value.what_changed_en: Replaced a single book citation by Väinö Mononen in the further reading section with a list of ten mostly self-published (Books on Demand) books by the same author, along with a stray phrase ('Kuolema kolkuttaa korvessa', meaning 'Death knocks in the wilderness'). The edit was reverted as self-publishing spam ('omakustannespämmiä').
evidence: *Mononen Väinö: ''Talvisota Kuhmossa I:'' Helsinki: Books on Demand, 2020. ISBN 978-952-80-2246-6.

value.what_changed_en: Added an unsourced sentence (with minor capitalization errors) claiming that Mussolini and especially Foreign Minister Ciano demanded arms shipments through Germany to Sweden and partly in secret onward to the Finnish front. Another editor reverted the addition as unsourced ("lähteetön").
evidence: Mussolini ja varsinkin ulkoministeri Ciano vaativat asekuljetuksia saksan läpi ruotsiin ja edelleen osittain salassa Suomen rintamalle.
value.claim_en: Benito Mussolini and especially Italian Foreign Minister Galeazzo Ciano demanded that arms shipments be allowed through Germany to Sweden and partly secretly onward to the Finnish front during the Winter War.
value.claim_fi: Benito Mussolini ja varsinkin Italian ulkoministeri Galeazzo Ciano vaativat asekuljetuksia Saksan läpi Ruotsiin ja edelleen osittain salassa Suomen rintamalle talvisodan aikana.

value.what_changed_en: Added two unsourced sentences stating that Häyhä kept snow in his mouth to reduce visible breath vapour and poured water over the snow at his firing position so it would not puff up when shooting. The edit was reverted with the summary 'lähteetöntä' ('unsourced').
evidence: Hän piti myös lunta suussaan vähentääkseen suusta tulevaa vesihöyryä, joka saattoi paljastaa hänen olinpaikkansa.
Hän kaatoi ampumisalustan lumen päälle vettä, jotta lumi ei pöllähtäisi hänen ampuessaan.
value.claim_en: Simo Häyhä kept snow in his mouth to reduce breath condensation and poured water onto the snow at his firing position to prevent snow puffs when firing.
value.claim_fi: Simo Häyhä piti lunta suussaan vähentääkseen hengityshöyryä ja kaatoi vettä ampuma-asemansa lumelle estääkseen lumen pöllähtämisen laukaistessa.
value.uncertainty_note: Both anecdotes are widely repeated in popular literature about Häyhä (though the snow-in-mouth story has been questioned by some biographers like Tapio Saarelainen, while freezing the snow bank is well-attested); either way, the addition was a sincere contribution reverted solely for lacking a citation.

value.what_changed_en: Added unsourced claims that some people speak of Simo Häyhä having thousands of sniper kills, noted that he was born into a family of eight children, and inserted a popular anecdote about him sending a letter after waking up wounded saying 'Stop the funeral! The deceased is missing!'
evidence: Mutta jotkut puhuvat jopa tuhansista kaadoista!
lisäykset tuosta muustakin yhteydestä tutusta "vainaja puuttuu" legendasta
value.claim_en: Some claim Simo Häyhä killed thousands of enemy soldiers, he was born into an eight-child family, and after waking from his injury he wrote a letter to his relatives saying 'Stop the funeral! The deceased is missing!'
value.claim_fi: Joidenkin mukaan Simo Häyhä ampui jopa tuhansia vihollissotilaita, hän syntyi kahdeksanlapsiseen perheeseen ja herättyään haavoittumisensa jälkeen hän lähetti läheisilleen kirjeen tekstillä "Hautajaiset seis! Vainaja puuttuu!"
value.narrative_en: Heroic mythologisation of Simo Häyhä
value.historical_note_en: Historical estimates of Simo Häyhä's sniper kills during the Winter War consistently place the total around 500 to 542 (plus possible submachine gun kills), not in the thousands.
value.uncertainty_note: The editor did include one accurate detail (he had seven siblings, making an eight-child family), suggesting this could also be viewed as a good-faith addition of popular folklore and hyperbole rather than deliberate fabrication, though the reverted claims distort established facts.

value.what_changed_en: Replaced Soviet commander Aleksei Vinogradov's name in the infobox with a vulgarity meaning 'asshole' ('persesilmäääääääääääääääää'), changed Finnish casualties from ~400 to ~0, and changed Soviet killed in action from 1,001 to 1,001,000,000.

Inserted a profanity and a derogatory ethnic slur for Russians into the infobox's note parameter, stating that 'a hell of a lot of Russkies died, at least 10,000', while also breaking the parameter name.
evidence: huomautuus ryssää kuoli aivan perkeleesti, ainakin 10 000     =
value.claim_en: At least 10,000 Soviet soldiers died in the Battle of Kollaa.
value.claim_fi: Kollaan taistelussa kuoli vähintään 10 000 neuvostosotilasta.

value.what_changed_en: Changed the description of Simo Häyhä's sniper kills from being 'estimated at up to 542 men, though a more accurate estimate is probably around 200 soldiers' to being 'proven to be 542 men', while accidentally corrupting the citation tag with the digits '2002'. The reverter noted that the change did not match the cited source.
evidence: joskin oikeampi arvio lienee noin 200 sotilasta.
value.claim_en: Simo Häyhä killed a proven 542 Red Army soldiers during the Winter War.
value.claim_fi: Simo Häyhän talvisodassa ampumien puna-armeijan sotilaiden määrä on todistetusti 542 miestä.
value.narrative_en: Mythologising Finnish Winter War heroes
value.historical_note_en: Historians such as Risto Marjomaa consider the widely circulated figure of 505–542 sniper kills for Simo Häyhä to be exaggerated wartime propaganda or unverified counting, estimating the actual number of sniper kills at closer to 200.
value.uncertainty_note: Because the edit kept the existing citation (while breaking its markup with '2002') so that it misrepresented what Marjomaa 2004 says, 'source_manipulation' or 'pov_push' are also strong candidates; '2002' could alternatively point to trollish number-inflation vandalism that got garbled during editing.

value.what_changed_en: Inserted colloquial, profane nationalist boasting stating that the Soviet Union got beaten up in the Winter War, that Finland won overwhelmingly, and that the Soviet Union should 'fuck off from the world map'.
evidence: Neuvostoliitto saisi painua vittuuun maailman kartalta
value.claim_en: Finland overwhelmingly won the Winter War and beat the Soviet Union so badly that it still suffers from it today.
value.claim_fi: Suomi voitti talvisodan ylivoimaisesti ja kukisti Neuvostoliiton niin pahasti, että se kärsii siitä vielä nykyäänkin.
value.narrative_en: Finnish nationalist triumphalism and anti-Soviet sentiment
value.historical_note_en: Although Finland preserved its independence and inflicted heavy losses on the Red Army, the Winter War ended with the Moscow Peace Treaty in March 1940, in which Finland was forced to cede significant territory to the Soviet Union; moreover, the Soviet Union dissolved in 1991.

value.what_changed_en: Changed several numerical figures in the article (including Finnish troop strength from 250,000 to 330,000), inserted unformatted plain-text citations to a book ('Talvisotakirja' by Gummerus), and reordered the words in a map caption, while only mentioning the caption word-order change in the edit summary.
value.claim_en: Finland's troop strength and other Winter War numerical figures were higher than previously stated, according to the book Talvisotakirja.
value.claim_fi: Suomen joukkojen vahvuus ja muut talvisodan luvut olivat aiemmin esitettyä suurempia Talvisotakirjan mukaan.
value.uncertainty_note: The diff omits the surrounding text for the changed numbers other than 250 (250,000 men in the infobox), and it appears to collapse multiple consecutive edits (as suggested by the revert summary). The editor likely tried in good faith to update figures using a real history book (ISBN 951-20-6674-2) with poor wikitext formatting while leaving existing conflicting citations intact, though deliberate misrepresentation cannot be completely ruled out without seeing the full diff.

value.what_changed_en: Replaced a portion of text describing Soviet food rations during the battle with random keyboard mashing, accompanied by a gibberish edit summary.

Rewrote the introductory definitions of Karelia across multiple edits: replaced 'there are two Karelias in the Karelia region' with 'the Karelia region is divided between Finland and Russia', removed the equating of Russian Karelia with 'East Karelia' (arguing Ladoga Karelia is not East Karelia), added detailed caveats about what the historical province of Karelia includes (such as areas ceded by Finland in 1940/1944 and Leningrad Oblast), and removed small coat-of-arms images.
evidence: Laatokan Karjala on kiistatta Venäjän Karjalaa, mutta ei Itä-Karjalaa
Karjalan alue jakautuu Suomen ja Venäjän kesken.
Osa aikaisemmin Suomelle kuulunutta Karjalaa, erityisesti [[Karjalan kannas]], kuuluu [[Leningradin oblasti]]in
value.claim_en: Karelia is divided between Finland and Russia such that Russian Karelia is not synonymous with East Karelia because it also includes Ladoga Karelia and parts of the Karelian Isthmus formerly belonging to Finland.
value.claim_fi: Karjalan alue jakautuu Suomen ja Venäjän kesken siten, ettei Venäjän Karjala ole sama asia kuin Itä-Karjala, koska siihen kuuluu myös aiemmin Suomelle kuuluneita Laatokan Karjalan ja Karjalankannaksen alueita.
value.narrative_en: Traditional Finnish historical-geographical distinction between ceded Finnish Karelia and East Karelia
value.uncertainty_note: Both sides accuse each other of POV-pushing in the edit summaries, as defining whether ceded Ladoga Karelia now counts as 'East Karelia' touches on national-historical terminology, making pov_push a plausible secondary fit.

value.what_changed_en: Inserted a snide editorial comment directly into the article body claiming there is a compound-word error in the article's title and mocking Finnish nationalists ('defenders of the fatherland', intentionally misspelled as internet slang 'isäm maan pulustajien').
evidence: Otsikossa yhdyssanavirhe, onko tämä isäm maan pulustajien itseironiaa?
value.claim_en: The article title 'Raatteen tien taistelu' contains a compound-word error.
value.claim_fi: Artikkelin otsikossa 'Raatteen tien taistelu' on yhdyssanavirhe.

value.what_changed_en: In the battle infobox, the editor changed the destroyed Soviet force from singular "division" to plural "divisions", increased Soviet casualties from 17,500 to 20,000 while adding citation-needed tags, and inserted an unreliable or fabricated source citation ("Markus Juutila: the Winter War, my grandfather's stories"). The reverter rolled it back asking "what on earth kind of source is that?"
evidence: Palautettu, mikä ihmeen lähde tuo on?
value.claim_en: Multiple Soviet divisions were destroyed in the Battle of Raate Road, and Soviet casualties amounted to 20,000.
value.claim_fi: Raatteen tien taistelussa tuhottiin useita Neuvostoliiton divisioonia ja neuvostotappiot olivat 20 000.
value.historical_note_en: In the Battle of Raate Road itself, one Soviet division (the 44th Rifle Division) was destroyed, whereas the 163rd Rifle Division had been defeated earlier in the wider Battle of Suomussalmi.
value.uncertainty_note: It is unclear whether the editor was acting in naive good faith (citing oral family stories or an unpublished text while misunderstanding {{Lähde}} tags) or deliberately inserting a fabricated joke source alongside inflated figures; false_factual_claim or good_faith_error would also be plausible.

value.what_changed_en: Removed the characterization 'radikaali' ('radical') from the Greater Finland ideology, changed 'mahdollisesti' ('possibly') to 'harvemmin' ('more rarely') regarding claims on Norwegian and Swedish territories, and added a claim that lack of broad Finnish aid to the East Karelian uprising was partly due to internal fragmentation following the White Terror. To back up this added claim, the editor inserted a bogus citation pointing to the generic homepage of the President of Finland with future dates, while claiming in the edit summary to be a docent.
evidence: Syy siihen, miksi Suomesta ei saatu laajaa apua johtuu osittain Suomen sisäisestä fragmentoitumisesta Valkoisen Terrorin jälkeen.
Minä olen dosentti! Aatteen radikaalius on tunnetusti hyvinkin subjektiivinen
value.claim_en: Greater Finland was not a radical ideology, rarely included Norwegian and Swedish territories, and failed to receive broad support during the East Karelian uprising partly due to Finland's internal fragmentation after the White Terror.
value.claim_fi: Suur-Suomi-aate ei ollut radikaali, siihen kuuluivat harvemmin Norjan ja Ruotsin alueet, ja laajan avun puuttuminen Itä-Karjalan kansannousussa johtui osittain Suomen sisäisestä hajanaisuudesta valkoisen terrorin jälkeen.
value.narrative_en: Softening the Greater Finland ideology and emphasizing the impact of the 1918 White Terror
value.uncertainty_note: The edit combines POV-pushing (removing 'radical', emphasizing the White Terror) with clear source manipulation (citing the generic homepage presidentti.fi with impossible future dates in March 2026 for an edit made in January 2026, which the reverter specifically flagged as not matching the source); 'pov_push' or 'vandalism'/trolling (given 'Minä olen dosentti!' and fake dates) are strong secondary aspects.

value.what_changed_en: As part of an ongoing back-and-forth revert war over the lead section's definitions and maps, the editor restored a contested map and table ('Suomen ja Venäjän Karjalat') alongside an alternative map ('Many Karelias.png') and expanded definitions of the regions of Karelia. Another editor later reverted it, citing the custom map as original research ('omaa tutkimusta').
evidence: Palautettu mm. kartta, jonka tietoa ei mitenkään ole osoitettu virheelliseksi.
value.claim_en: The geographical and administrative divisions of Finnish and Russian Karelia correspond to the specific subregions and municipal boundaries depicted in the user-created map and table.
value.claim_fi: Suomen ja Venäjän Karjalan maantieteellinen ja hallinnollinen jako vastaa käyttäjän laatimassa kartassa ja taulukossa esitettyjä osa-alueita ja kuntarajoja.
value.uncertainty_note: The edit summary appears to concatenate multiple edits in a revert chain, showing a dispute over whether the custom map 'Suomen ja Venäjän Karjalat.png' and certain municipal inclusions constitute original research or match the cited sources.

value.what_changed_en: Added a custom map dividing the Republic of Karelia into historical subregions (such as Olonets Karelia, Ladoga Karelia, and White Karelia) mapped onto modern administrative districts, changed the verb 'ceded' (luovutti) to 'was forced to cede' (pakkoluovutti), and removed unreferenced/citation-needed tags.
evidence: virheellinen kartta pois, katso tarkemmin keskustelusivu
value.claim_en: Russian Karelia (the Republic of Karelia) consists of specific historical subregions corresponding directly to sets of modern districts, and Finland was forced to cede territory.
value.claim_fi: Venäjän Karjala eli Karjalan tasavalta jakautuu tiettyihin nykyisiä hallintopiirejä vastaaviin historiallisiin alueisiin, ja Suomi pakkoluovutti alueita.
value.narrative_en: Finnish irredentist or nationalist framing of Karelian historical geography and World War II territorial cessions
value.uncertainty_note: The edit spans multiple issues at once: an ongoing edit war over an allegedly inaccurate/original-research map of Karelian historical regions (content_dispute / false_factual_claim), changing 'ceded' to 'forced to cede' (pov_push), and removing citation-needed templates without adding sources (source_manipulation).

value.what_changed_en: Replaced the Finnish name of the Soviet-backed Finnish Democratic Republic from 'Suomen kansanvaltainen tasavalta' (using the native Finnish word for democratic) to 'Suomen demokraattinen tasavalta' (using the loanword) across multiple mentions and links. The reverter undid this, arguing that contemporary documents used 'kansanvaltainen'.
value.claim_en: The Finnish name of the Terijoki Government's proclaimed state was 'Suomen demokraattinen tasavalta' rather than 'Suomen kansanvaltainen tasavalta'.
value.claim_fi: Terijoen hallituksen julistaman valtion suomenkielinen nimi oli Suomen demokraattinen tasavalta eikä Suomen kansanvaltainen tasavalta.
value.historical_note_en: Contemporary Finnish-language Soviet documents from 1939–1940, such as the December 1939 treaty, officially titled the entity 'Suomen Kansanvaltainen Tasavalta', though 'Suomen demokraattinen tasavalta' also appears in later Finnish usage as a back-translation from Russian.
value.uncertainty_note: Could also be classified as good_faith_error if the editor simply assumed 'demokraattinen tasavalta' was the standard name (or was fixing links after a page move), rather than engaging in an active naming dispute.

value.what_changed_en: As part of an ongoing edit war, the editor rewrote definitions of Karelia's subregions to equate Russian Karelia (including Ladoga Karelia) with East Karelia, framed the region around administrative borders (claiming the Karelian Isthmus was separated from Karelia in 1944), adjusted coat-of-arms images, and removed a citation-needed tag.
evidence: Laatokan Karjala on toki Itä-Karjalaa, sillä Itä-Karjala = Venäjän Karjala = Karjalan tasavalta
Marraskuussa 1944 koko Karjalankannaksen alue erotettiin Karjalasta ja siirrettiin osaksi
value.claim_en: Russian Karelia (the Republic of Karelia, including Ladoga Karelia) is synonymous with East Karelia, and the Karelian Isthmus was separated from Karelia when transferred to Leningrad Oblast in 1944.
value.claim_fi: Venäjän Karjala (Karjalan tasavalta, mukaan lukien Laatokan Karjala) on sama asia kuin Itä-Karjala, ja Karjalankannas erotettiin Karjalasta siirrettäessä osaksi Leningradin aluetta vuonna 1944.
value.narrative_en: Redefining historical Karelian regions along post-WWII administrative borders
value.historical_note_en: In standard Finnish geographical and historical terminology, East Karelia (Itä-Karjala) refers to Aunus and Viena Karelia east of the pre-1939 border, distinct from Ladoga Karelia (Laatokan Karjala) which was ceded by Finland in 1940/1944.
value.uncertainty_note: The input aggregates multiple edits and reverts from a multi-round 3RR edit war. While one reverter labeled it 'vandalistista POV-pushausta', others called it 'räikeä asiavirhe' (blatant factual error) and clumsy wording over geographical vs. administrative definitions, so 'pov_push' or 'false_factual_claim' are also strong candidates.

value.what_changed_en: Inserted a talk-page-style complaint directly into the beginning of the article's lead text (breaking bold formatting), stating that a significant portion of the article's information is wrong, and giving examples that the Battle of Raate Road ended on January 7 and the 163rd Division had already retreated from the main village in December.
evidence: Esim Raatteen tien taistelu loppui 7.tammikuuta. 163 divisioona oli vetäytynyt kirkonkylätstä jo joulukuussa.
value.claim_en: The Battle of Raate Road ended on January 7, and the Soviet 163rd Division had already retreated from the village of Suomussalmi in December.
value.claim_fi: Raatteen tien taistelu päättyi 7. tammikuuta ja Neuvostoliiton 163. divisioona oli vetäytynyt Suomussalmen kirkonkylästä jo joulukuussa.

value.what_changed_en: In bundled edits across Karelian region articles (Vienan Karjala and Laatokan Karjala), the editor added etymologies deriving 'Viena' from Russian 'Dvina' cited to blogs and user-generated wikis, reframed Ladoga Karelia primarily as a current Russian region rather than a ceded historical Finnish province, and inserted neologism translations like 'Pohjois-"Laatokkala"' ('North Ladoga-land'). Revertees rejected the changes due to unreliable sources, invented terms, and block evasion.
evidence: palautus: roskalähde | Kumottu muokkaus 11780042, jonka teki 193.64.x.x (keskustelu) | rv, itsekeksittyjä Laatokkaloita | Estetyn käyttäjän muokkauksia
value.claim_en: The Finnish name Viena derives from the Russian river name (Severnaya) Dvina, and Ladoga Karelia is primarily defined as a contemporary Russian territory (also translatable as 'Laatokkala') rather than a historical Finnish province.
value.claim_fi: Viena-nimi on johdettu Vienanjoen venäjänkielisestä nimestä (Severnaja) Dvina, ja Laatokan Karjala määritellään ensisijaisesti nykyiseksi Venäjän alueeksi (myös nimellä "Laatokkala") historiallisen suomalaisen maakunnan osan sijaan.
value.narrative_en: Emphasising Russian nomenclature and contemporary Russian administrative framing of Karelian regions
value.uncertainty_note: The input data aggregates edits and summaries from two different articles (Vienan Karjala and Laatokan Karjala) by a blocked sockpuppet; the edits combine Russian-centric reframing (pov_push), original research/neologisms, and poor blog/wiki sourcing (source_manipulation).

value.what_changed_en: Removed a section titled 'Käkisalmi is nowadays Priozersk' containing a Russian quote and external link about the 1948 renaming, while updating the historical Russian name periods and typography in the lead section as part of a naming dispute.
evidence: Nimenmuutoksen toteaminen samoin kuin Primorskin (ent. Koivisto) artikkelissa
value.claim_en: Between 1918 and 1940 the Russian name of the town was Kjakisalmi rather than Keksgolm, and Käkisalmi remains the valid Finnish exonym rather than having been replaced by Priozersk.
value.claim_fi: Vuosina 1918–1940 kaupungin venäjänkielinen nimi oli Kjakisalmi eikä Keksgolm, ja Käkisalmi on edelleen käypä suomenkielinen nimi sen sijaan, että nimi olisi korvautunut Priozerskilla.
value.narrative_en: Finnish Wikipedia naming dispute over ceded Karelian place names
value.uncertainty_note: Touches on nationalist/linguistic framing (pov_push) regarding whether Soviet-era Russian renamings supersede traditional Finnish names in Finnish usage, which was a classic Wikipedia policy dispute around 2006.

value.what_changed_en: The edit replaced phrasing like 'remained to Finland' (Suomelle jääneet) with 'stayed in Finland' (Suomessa pysyneet) to emphasize that municipal territories rather than administrative municipalities were ceded, removed a reference to Border Karelia (Raja-Karjala) in favor of more detailed geographical descriptions, and added a map of ceded Karelia. Reverter summaries dismissed the wording changes as pedantic nitpicking and restored the previous phrasing.
evidence: Yhtäkään luovutetun Karjalan kuntaa ei hallinnollisena kuntana luovutettu, vaan niiden alueet.
Pois WPK:n (?) satuilu Laatokan Karjalasta erillisestä Raja-Karjalasta.
value.claim_en: The territories rather than the administrative municipalities of Karelia were ceded to the Soviet Union, unceded parts stayed in Finland rather than being left to it, and Border Karelia is not distinct from Ladoga Karelia.
value.claim_fi: Neuvostoliitolle luovutettiin Karjalan kuntien alueet eikä hallinnollisia kuntia, luovuttamattomat osat pysyivät Suomessa eivätkä jääneet sille, eikä Raja-Karjala ole Laatokan Karjalasta erillinen alue.
value.uncertainty_note: The editor may be a known block-evading pedantic user (often associated with WPK disputes on Finnish Wikipedia), and the insistence on 'stayed in Finland' vs 'left to Finland' touches slightly on legalistic framing, which borders on minor pov_push.

value.what_changed_en: Reordered and expanded the foreign-language names in the lead sentence, placing the current Russian name Priozersk first, formatting the Karelian name with a language template, and adding specific year ranges for the historical Russian names Keksgolm (1611–1918 and 1940–1948) and Kjakisalmi (1918–1940).
value.claim_en: In Russian, the town is called Priozersk, and was known as Keksgolm in 1611–1918 and 1940–1948, and as Kjakisalmi in 1918–1940.
value.claim_fi: Kaupunki on venäjäksi Priozersk, ja sen venäjänkielinen nimi oli vuosina 1611–1918 ja 1940–1948 Keksgolm sekä vuosina 1918–1940 Kjakisalmi.
value.uncertainty_note: During 1941–1944 (Continuation War) the town was recaptured by Finland, making the 1940–1948 range slightly simplified regarding actual administration, though it reflects Soviet naming.

value.what_changed_en: Inserted a list of bordering bodies of water (Gulf of Finland, Saimaa, Ladoga, Onega, and the White Sea) into the lead definition of Karelia, arguing in an edit war against a reverter who objected that the phrasing was not in the cited source and distorted its meaning.
evidence: Miksi Karjalan suuria 'reunavesistöjä' ei saisi luetella? | Ei sisälly lähteeseen, vääristää ajatusta?! Höpö, höpö!
value.claim_en: Karelia is located between the Gulf of Finland, Lake Saimaa, Lake Ladoga, Lake Onega, and the White Sea, mostly in eastern Fennoscandia.
value.claim_fi: Karjala sijaitsee Suomenlahden, Saimaan, Laatokan, Äänisen ja Vienanmeren välillä, valtaosin Fennoskandian itäosassa.
value.uncertainty_note: Because the added text was placed into a sentence backed by an existing citation, this also borders on source_manipulation (source-text integrity), though the editor appears to be sincerely arguing over geographical phrasing rather than deliberately faking a source.

value.what_changed_en: Redefined the northwestern boundary of the Karelian Isthmus as a line from Juustilanselkä to Pekonlahti (slightly inside the Republic of Karelia), removed a map of the isthmus, and altered historical wording throughout the article (such as changing 'ended up in Russia' to 'passed to the Russian Empire', 'Soviet Russia' to 'Russia', and 'independent [Russia]' to 'post-Soviet [Russia]'). The edit was a revert by a block-evading user.
value.claim_en: The northwestern boundary of the Karelian Isthmus runs from Juustilanselkä to Pekonlahti on Lake Ladoga, placing a small part of the isthmus in the southwesternmost part of the Republic of Karelia.
value.claim_fi: Karjalankannaksen luoteisraja kulkee Juustilanselältä Laatokan Pekonlahteen siten, että pieni osa kannaksesta sijaitsee Karjalan tasavallan lounaisimmassa osassa.
value.uncertainty_note: Only the opening paragraphs are shown in the context, so the exact sentences modified further down in the article (concerning South Karelia, Kymenlaakso, South Savo, and Soviet/post-Soviet Russia) are reconstructed from the diff fragments; the reverter reverted strictly on grounds of block evasion by a known sockpuppeteer (WPK).

value.what_changed_en: Removed mentions of the Greater Finland ideology having imperialist traits and Finnicization policies by Finnish Reds in Soviet Karelia, replacing them with sections arguing that the movement was a humanitarian effort to save Finnic peoples from Stalinist Russification and liquidation, and added a disputed-neutrality tag.
evidence: imperialismi eli siirtomaavalta -käsitteenä ei kuulu Suur-Suomeen
Toisaalta 30-luvulla aate alkoi saada selvemmin imperialistisia piirteitä.
Suur-Suomen toteuttamatta jättäminen altisti nämä kansat turvattomuuden tilaan, josta syystä nykyään karjalan, suomen ja vepsän kielen osaaminen Karjalan tasavallassa on vain vanhusten taitona.
value.claim_en: The Greater Finland ideology was not imperialist, but rather a humanitarian effort to protect Finnic peoples from Soviet Russification and Stalinist purges, and the failure to realize it caused the decline of Finnic languages in Karelia.
value.claim_fi: Suur-Suomi-aate ei ollut imperialistinen, vaan inhimillinen pyrkimys suojella suomensukuisia kansoja neuvostoliittolaiselta venäläistämiseltä ja Stalinin puhdistuksilta, ja sen toteuttamatta jääminen johti suomensukuisten kielten taantumiseen Karjalassa.
value.narrative_en: Apologetics and justification for the Greater Finland ideology
value.historical_note_en: Mainstream historiography recognizes that 1930s and wartime Greater Finland ideology included expansionist and nationalist ambitions alongside kinship motives, and that early Soviet nationality policy in Karelia (korenizatsiya) initially promoted Finnish through Red Finnish leadership before turning to Russification and purges in the late 1930s.
value.uncertainty_note: The data aggregates a multi-step edit war (7 reverts) into a single entry, so some removed and inserted spans reflect intermediate compromise attempts alongside the main POV-pushing text.

value.what_changed_en: In a series of back-and-forth edits on the 1920s–1930s Soviet Karelia section, the editor added a claim that people in White Karelia (Vienan Karjala) were satisfied with the Finnish language, added a mention of leader Edvard Gylling's socialist dream, and removed a sentence stating that Finnish Reds strongly Finnicised Soviet Karelia (claiming it was repetitive). The reverter undid the changes, accusing the editor of adding an unfounded claim and removing essential information about Finnicisation by the Reds during an ongoing dispute.
evidence: Vienan Karjalassa taas suomen kieleen oltiin tyytyväisiä, koska vienan karjalalla oli enemmän vaikutteita suomesta.
Karjalan johtaja Edvard Gylling toteutti unelmaa sosialistisesta työläisten valtiosta.
Neuvosto-Karjalaa suomalaistettiin suomalaisten punaisten johdolla voimakkaasti.
Palautettu, aivan perusteetta poistettu tietoja punaisten tekemästä suomalaistamisesta yms.
value.claim_en: Attitudes toward the Finnish language in Soviet Karelia were mixed, with residents of White Karelia being satisfied with it due to linguistic similarities while leader Edvard Gylling pursued a dream of a socialist workers' state.
value.claim_fi: Suhtautuminen suomen kieleen Neuvosto-Karjalassa oli moninaista: Vienan Karjalassa siihen oltiin tyytyväisiä kielellisten vaikutteiden vuoksi, ja johtaja Edvard Gylling toteutti unelmaa sosialistisesta työläisten valtiosta.
value.narrative_en: Softening the portrayal of Red Finnish Finnicisation policy in Soviet Karelia
value.uncertainty_note: The diff bundles multiple back-and-forth edits during an edit war, blurring the line between a content_dispute over paragraph structure/repetition and a pov_push softening the criticism of Finnish Reds' language policies in Soviet Karelia.

value.what_changed_en: The editor reverted to an older version of the article, changing wording from 'stayed in Finland' ('Suomessa pysyneet') to 'remained to Finland' ('Suomelle jääneet'), referring to ceded 'municipalities' rather than 'territories', and removing a map of ceded Karelia along with an expired protection template. The reverter undid this to restore the map and maintain precise legal phrasing that territories—not administrative municipalities—were ceded.
evidence: Yhtäkään luovutetun Karjalan kuntaa ei hallinnollisena kuntana luovutettu, vaan niiden alueet.

value.what_changed_en: Inserted a sentence using an anti-Russian ethnic slur ('ryssä') and profanity ('perkeleesti') claiming at least 10,000 Soviets died at Kollaa, followed by a nationalist slogan ('One Finn equals ten Russkies'). This combines deliberate vandalism (slurs and profanity) with nationalist POV-pushing and an unsourced casualty figure contradicting the infobox estimate of 8,000.
evidence: Kollaalla ryssää kuoli aivan perkeleesti, ainakin 10 000.
value.claim_en: At least 10,000 Soviet soldiers died at the Battle of Kollaa, demonstrating Finnish superiority.
value.claim_fi: Kollaan taistelussa kuoli ainakin 10 000 neuvostosotilasta, mikä osoitti suomalaisten ylivoimaisuutta.
value.narrative_en: Finnish nationalist glorification and anti-Russian sentiment regarding the Winter War
value.uncertainty_note: Overlaps with pov_push due to the nationalist slogan and glorification, and false_factual_claim due to contradicting the article's 8,000 casualty estimate, but the overt use of ethnic slurs and profanity makes vandalism the primary fit.

value.what_changed_en: Added a counter-argument after Sergey Lavrov's quote calling Karelian restitution pollsters 'provocateurs', stating that opponents of the occupation of the Baltic states were also once labeled provocateurs, and cited a 1985 newspaper article by Matti Vanhanen hosted on kavkaz.fi. The reverter noted that the source and the claim did not match (likely original synthesis using Vanhanen's 1985 Finlandization-era piece as an example rather than a secondary source making the comparison).
evidence: Toisaalta myös Baltian maiden miehityksen vastustajat pyrittiin aikanaan leimaamaan provokaattoreiksi.
value.claim_en: Opponents of the occupation of the Baltic states were previously sought to be labeled as provocateurs, analogously to advocates of Karelian restitution.
value.claim_fi: Myös Baltian maiden miehityksen vastustajat pyrittiin aikanaan leimaamaan provokaattoreiksi Karjalan palautuksen kannattajien tapaan.
value.narrative_en: Advocacy for the restitution of ceded Karelia / anti-Finlandization parallel
value.uncertainty_note: Also strongly overlaps with source_manipulation (original synthesis / source-claim mismatch as noted by the reverter), since a 1985 article by Matti Vanhanen could not itself draw a comparison to Lavrov's 2005 statement on Karelia, and instead appears to be used as a primary-source exhibit of such labeling.

value.what_changed_en: Modified four numerical figures (39 to 40, 3 to 5, 250 to 330, and 130 to 114), accidentally broke a book citation template, and appended three poorly formatted book titles. The reverter undid the edit, noting that unsourced suspicious information had been added.
evidence: }), Esko Kilpelä: Raatteentien kutsu, Talvisodan ääni.
value.uncertainty_note: Because the surrounding text for the four altered numbers (39->40, 3->5, 250->330, 130->114) is cut off from the context, it is unclear what exact statistics—likely aircraft counts or casualties given the aviation book titles—were changed, and whether this was deliberate falsification, source manipulation, or a clumsy good-faith attempt to update numbers using real books.

value.what_changed_en: Inserted a coined literal Finnish gloss ("Karjalan tai Pohjois-Laatokkala", roughly "Karelian or North Ladoga-land") for the Russian regional names Karelskoje Priladožje and Severnoje Priladožje. Another editor reverted it as an unsourced, awkward original translation.

value.claim_fi: Raja-Karjala muodosti Laatokan Karjalan itäosan, josta Suomi joutui luopumaan ja vetäytymään vuosina 1940 ja 1944, eikä sen kulttuuria luonnehtinut voimakas venäläisvaikutus.

value.historical_note_en: While the Karelian Isthmus was administratively transferred from the Karelo-Finnish SSR to Leningrad Oblast in 1944–1945, it continues to be regarded geographically and historically as part of the broader region of Karelia.
value.uncertainty_note: The edit mixes an idiosyncratic definitional dispute (conflating administrative units with the historical-geographic region of Karelia), unsourced folk-historical assertions ('good_faith_error' / 'false_factual_claim'), and slightly loaded phrasing ('venäläisten hallitsemaa' — 'ruled by Russians', hinting at 'pov_push').

value.claim_en: Supporters of Greater Finland sought to save Finnic peoples in Karelia from Soviet ethnic cleansing and Russification, though this motive is undermined by the linguistic and cultural assimilation of the Sámi in Finland.
value.claim_fi: Suur-Suomen kannattajat pyrkivät pelastamaan suomensukuiset kansat etnisiltä puhdistuksilta ja venäläistymiseltä, mutta motiivin asettaa kyseenalaiseksi saamelaisten suomalaistuminen Suomessa.

value.what_changed_en: Removed neutral text about arguments for and against the return of Karelia and inserted a lengthy, first-person manifesto and website links promoting irredentist organizations (such as Suur-Suomi r.y.) that demand the immediate return of ceded territories, repayment of war reparations, and war crimes trials for Russian leaders. It also argued in an editorializing tone that Karelia's Russian population consists of Russified minorities eager to assimilate into Finland.
evidence: Vaadimme Suomelta ryöstettyjen ns. sotakorvausten eli ryöstösaaliin takaisinmaksatusta
value.claim_en: Ceded Karelia is an occupied territory whose Russified minority populations would willingly assimilate into Finland, and Russia must immediately return the territories under the 1920 Treaty of Tartu, repay war reparations as loot, and face international prosecution for war crimes.
value.claim_fi: Luovutettu Karjala on miehitetty alue, jonka venäläistetyt vähemmistökansat sulautuisivat halukkaasti Suomeen, ja Venäjän on välittömästi palautettava alueet Tarton rauhansopimuksen mukaisesti, maksettava sotakorvaukset takaisin ryöstösaaliina sekä vastattava sotarikoksista.
value.narrative_en: Finnish irredentism (Greater Finland) and anti-Russian activism
value.historical_note_en: Ceded Karelia was formally transferred to the Soviet Union under the 1947 Paris Peace Treaty—which is an internationally recognized peace treaty rather than an 'occupation treaty'—and Finland's 1990 unilateral reinterpretation of its military sovereignty clauses did not alter territorial borders.

value.what_changed_en: Added the outer islands of the Gulf of Finland to the list of ceded territories from which evacuees came, adjusted compass directions for Kuusamo, Salla, and the Rybachy Peninsula (changing 'northwest' to 'northeast'), and removed a period from an image caption. The edit was reverted for block evasion ('eston kiertoa').

value.uncertainty_note: The edit combines minor copyediting, a valid addition (the Gulf of Finland islands), and a geographical error (changing northwest to northeast on Kalastajasaarento), while the community reverted it purely on procedural grounds (block evasion by a known long-term abuser 'WPK'), making it sit between 'other', 'content_dispute', and 'false_factual_claim'.

value.what_changed_en: Replaced the neutral wording that Finnish troops 'captured' (valtasivat) 'ceded' (luovutetun) Karelia in the Continuation War with phrasing stating they 'returned to Finnish control' or 'retook control of' Karelia 'lost in the Winter War as a result of the Soviet attack'. value.claim_fi: Suomalaisjoukot palauttivat hallintaansa Neuvostoliiton hyökkäyksen seurauksena talvisodassa menetetyn Karjalan sen sijaan, että olisivat vallanneet luovutetun alueen.

value.what_changed_en: Reverted an earlier change to restore the traditional Finnish name 'Käkisalmi' instead of the post-1948 Russian name 'Priozersk' as the primary name throughout the article's lead and image captions, while also expanding historical name variants.

value.uncertainty_note: In Finnish, 'Käkisalmi' is the standard exonym (recommended by Kotus and used as the article title on Finnish Wikipedia), whereas the reverting editor argues for recognizing the official post-1948 Russian name 'Priozersk'. Depending on how one views the revert war, it sits on the border between a standard naming convention content_dispute and mild nationalistic pov_push.

value.uncertainty_note: The edit makes seemingly plausible copyedits and historical additions (characteristic of a known banned Finnish Wikipedia sockpuppeteer who mass-edits geography/history articles), and it was reverted procedurally for block evasion rather than content issues; it could alternatively fit 'content_dispute' or 'good_faith_error' (e.g. shifting focus from Raja-Karjala to broader Laatokan Karjala and introducing a typo 'Viipurin kuvernementtiiin').

value.what_changed_en: Inserted a parenthetical historical rebuttal challenging the claim of millennia-old Finnish settlement in Karelia, arguing that pre-1617 inhabitants (outside Vyborg Karelia) were Orthodox Karelians who identified with Russians and were largely expelled by Sweden after the Treaty of Stolbovo. Over consecutive edits, the editor adjusted details like specifying Ladoga Karelia over the Karelian Isthmus before another editor reverted it as historically inaccurate and took the discussion to the talk page.

value.claim_en: Pre-war Finnish settlement in ceded Karelia outside Vyborg Karelia largely dates to after 1617, as the earlier Orthodox Karelian population identified more with Russians and was largely expelled by Sweden after the Treaty of Stolbovo.
value.claim_fi: Luovutetun Karjalan sotia edeltänyt suomalainen asutus Viipurin Karjalaa lukuun ottamatta on pitkälti vuoden 1617 jälkeistä perua, sillä aiempi ortodoksinen karjalaisväestö identifioitui enemmän venäläisiin ja karkotettiin suurelta osin Ruotsin toimesta Stolbovan rauhan jälkeen.
value.narrative_en: Challenging Finnish historical Continuity in Karelia
value.historical_note_en: Following the Treaty of Stolbovo in 1617, Sweden did not formally expel the Orthodox Karelian population by state decree, though tens of thousands fled to Russia (becoming the Tver Karelians) due to heavy taxation, Lutheran proselytization, and wartime reprisals.
value.uncertainty_note: The edit also fits false_factual_claim (regarding deliberate expulsion vs. flight/emigration) and pov_push (arguing against pro-restitution claims in editorial voice), making it a borderline case between those categories and content_dispute.

value.what_changed_en: In an ongoing revert war, the edit altered the presentation and order of Käkisalmi's foreign and historical names in the lead sentence: it moved the Karelian name after the Swedish name without a language template, listed the historical Russian name 'Keksgolm' ahead of the current official Russian name 'Priozersk' (marked as 'since 1948'), and removed the detailed timeline of Russian name changes between 1611 and 1948.
value.claim_en: In Russian, Käkisalmi is called Keksgolm, or since 1948 Priozersk, and until 1611 Korela.
value.claim_fi: Käkisalmi on venäjäksi Keksgolm eli vuodesta 1948 Priozersk, ja vuoteen 1611 Korela.
value.uncertainty_note: Giving precedence to the historical pre-1948 Russian name 'Keksgolm' over the current official Soviet-era name 'Priozersk' could reflect a nationalist/revanchist preference regarding ceded Karelia (pov_push), or simply an editorial disagreement over lead formatting and verbosity.

value.what_changed_en: Inserted a copy-pasted overview paragraph about the Winter War (likely from the Talvisota article) into the History section, while accidentally corrupting words and markup in the lead paragraph (replacing a non-breaking space with 'pienen' ('small') and breaking 'rauhansopimuksessa').

value.what_changed_en: Reorganised and reworded the bulleted list of Finnish territories ceded after the Winter War in 1940, splitting the outer islands of the Gulf of Finland into western and eastern groups (with a typo 'tyhmä' for 'ryhmä'), removing the mention of Orthodox Border Karelia, and adding references to southeastern parts of North Karelia. The edit was reverted as block evasion ('eston kiertoa').
value.claim_en: The territories ceded by Finland in 1940 can be grouped by dividing the Gulf of Finland outer islands into western and eastern groups and distinguishing the ceded southeastern parts of North Karelia alongside Ladoga Karelia.
value.claim_fi: Suomen vuonna 1940 luovuttamat aluekokonaisuudet jakautuvat muun muassa Suomenlahden ulkosaarten läntiseen ja itäiseen ryhmään, lähes koko Laatokan Karjalaan sekä Pohjois-Karjalan kaakkois- ja itäosiin.
value.uncertainty_note: The edit was reverted on procedural grounds for block evasion ('eston kiertoa') rather than for overt falsehood or vandalism; it mixes geographical re-categorisation, minor factual/terminological tweaks (e.g. modern region Pohjois-Karjala vs. historical Raja-Karjala), and a typo ('tyhmä'), so good_faith_error or other could also fit.

value.what_changed_en: Reworded geographical and administrative descriptions of Ladoga Karelia (such as changing 'most of' to 'practically entirely', adding details on municipal mergers like Tuupovaara joining Joensuu in 2005, and adding a disambiguation note about Central Karelia). The edit was reverted solely on procedural grounds as block evasion ('rv, eston kiertoa').

value.claim_fi: Vanha Laatokan Karjala luovutettiin käytännössä kokonaan, sen Suomessa pysyneet pienet alueet tulivat osaksi Etelä- ja Pohjois-Karjalaa (Tuupovaaran liittyessä Joensuuhun 2005), eikä entistä Keski-Karjalaa pidä sekoittaa nykyiseen Keski-Karjalan seutukuntaan.
